units.t: Persuasion & Rhetoric. Episode one.
In this episode: Aristotle's rhetoric: ethos, pathos, logos, Why stories persuade and What makes a great speech.
Part one. Aristotle's rhetoric: ethos, pathos, logos.
Every ad you scroll past and every speech that moves you is using tools Aristotle catalogued about 2,300 years ago.
Persuasion as a science.
In Athens in the 300s BC, citizens argued their own court cases and voted directly in the assembly, so speaking well was a survival skill.
Paid teachers called sophists taught it, and critics like Plato worried they made the weaker argument look stronger.
Aristotle took a different approach.
In his Rhetoric, he studied persuasion the way a scientist studies animals, defining it as seeing the available means of persuasion in any case.
He named three modes of proof: ethos, pathos and logos.
Good persuasion usually combines them.
Perfect logic from someone we distrust falls flat, and pure emotion fades once the feeling wears off.
Ethos and pathos.
Ethos is the speaker's credibility.
Aristotle said we trust speakers who show practical wisdom, good character and goodwill towards us.
These are perceptions a speaker builds.
A tradie mentioning 20 years on the tools, a politician rolling up their sleeves at a flood site, or someone admitting a weakness are all building ethos.
It can also be borrowed, which is why companies pay celebrities to endorse products.
Pathos is stirring emotions such as fear, pity, anger or hope, because people judge differently when they feel differently.
It becomes a problem only when emotion replaces reasons.
Australia's graphic cigarette-pack warnings, required since 2006 and enlarged under 2012 plain packaging laws, make the risk feel real.
Logos and enthymemes.
Logos covers facts, examples, statistics and logical steps.
Aristotle noticed that everyday arguments rarely spell out every premise.
He called these shortened arguments enthymemes.
'Buy this car, it has a five-star safety rating' leaves out the premise 'you want a safe car', which the audience fills in themselves.
That participation is part of what makes enthymemes persuasive.
It also makes them a good place to hide weak assumptions.
When you hear a punchy argument, try saying the missing premise out loud and ask whether you actually agree with it.
Fitting the occasion.
Kairos is often added to Aristotle's three.
It is a broader Greek idea, linked to earlier teachers such as Gorgias, meaning the right message at the right moment.
Home insurance pitches land differently the week after a storm, and a barbecue joke can sink a eulogy.
That is why sunscreen ads peak in summer and gym ads flood January.
Aristotle also sorted speeches by purpose.
Deliberative speeches argue about the future, such as a budget pitch.
Forensic speeches argue about the past, as in court.
Epideictic speeches praise or blame in the present: eulogies, toasts and award speeches.
Knowing which you are giving helps you choose your tools.
Spotting it in the wild.
Try this on the next ad or speech you meet.
Ethos: who is speaking, and is the credibility earned or borrowed?
Pathos: what am I being made to feel, and does the feeling match the facts?
Logos: what is the actual claim, what evidence supports it, and what premise is unstated?
Kairos: why is this reaching me now?
You will find most effective messages lean on one mode more than the others.
The skill cuts both ways.
It makes you harder to fool, and it makes you a clearer, fairer speaker yourself.
The key idea: Aristotle's Rhetoric is the earliest surviving systematic study of persuasion, built on three modes of proof: ethos, character, pathos, emotion, and logos, reasoning.
Part two. Why stories persuade.
Facts tell, stories sell.
There's real psychology behind why a good story can change a mind that statistics couldn't.
Minds built for narrative.
Long before writing, people passed on knowledge through stories: where the water was, which plants were dangerous, who could be trusted.
Aboriginal Australians have kept oral traditions going for many thousands of years, and some researchers argue certain stories preserve memories of real events such as rising seas.
A story gives information a shape: someone wanted something, something got in the way, and something changed.
That shape makes facts easier to remember and repeat.
Psychologists note that a list of facts is quickly forgotten, while the same facts inside a narrative tend to stick.
Transported, and off guard.
In 2000, psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock described 'narrative transportation': the feeling of being carried away into a story.
People who were more absorbed were more likely to adopt beliefs consistent with the story, and less likely to pick holes in it.
Given a list of arguments, we naturally counter-argue.
Following a character, we are busy wondering what happens next.
That lowered guard is why a single dramatic anecdote can outweigh solid data.
As an audience, ask whether a story is typical or just vivid, and what the numbers say.
One face beats a million.
In a well-known 2007 study, Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic asked people to donate to a charity.
Some read about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl from Mali facing hunger.
Others read statistics about millions of people facing food shortages in Africa.
The Rokia group gave significantly more.
Strikingly, adding the statistics to Rokia's story reduced donations.
This 'identifiable victim effect' explains why charities lead with one person's story.
It is also a reminder that our compassion doesn't scale well with numbers, which matters when big problems are at stake.
The shape of a story.
In 1863, German writer Gustav Freytag described a pattern in plays now called Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.
Screenwriters often simplify it to three acts.
The engine in every version is conflict.
'I went to the shop and bought milk' isn't a story; 'the shop was closed and the baby was screaming' starts to become one.
Kurt Vonnegut liked to graph a hero's fortune over time.
In 2016, University of Vermont researchers tracked the emotional tone of 1,327 novels and found six core arcs: rags to riches, tragedy, man in a hole, Icarus, Cinderella and Oedipus.
Icarus, Oedipus and a double 'man in a hole' were among the most downloaded.
Using stories well.
A common mistake is casting your company as the hero.
Audiences care most about their own problems.
Marketers reframe the hero's journey so the customer is the hero and the brand is the wise guide, like Obi-Wan Kenobi.
A bank ad showing a young couple collecting the keys to their first home follows this pattern.
At work, try situation, complication, resolution: here's where we are, here's what went wrong, here's what to do.
A two-minute story about one real customer can win more support than twenty slides of data.
Use the story to open the door and the evidence to hold it open.
The key idea: People remember and pass on information more easily when it comes as a story, because a story gives facts a shape.
Part three. What makes a great speech.
A two-minute address at a cemetery, a hot August afternoon in Washington, a park in Redfern.
Why some speeches outlive the people who gave them.
Brevity and defiance.
On 19 November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a military cemetery at Gettysburg, months after one of the bloodiest battles of the American Civil War.
The main speaker, Edward Everett, talked for about two hours.
Lincoln spoke for two minutes, roughly 270 words, reaching back to 1776 and framing the war as a test of whether a nation built on equality could survive.
In May and June 1940, new Prime Minister Winston Churchill offered the Commons 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' and called Dunkirk a colossal military disaster.
His repeated 'we shall fight' is anaphora: repeating the opening words of successive phrases to build momentum.
King's dream.
On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
Martin Luther King Jr began with a prepared text, using the metaphor of America handing Black citizens a bad cheque marked 'insufficient funds'.
Partway through, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson reportedly called out for him to tell them about the dream.
King moved into a passage he had used in earlier sermons.
The repeated line 'I have a dream' replaced an abstract demand with concrete pictures of a fairer future, blending biblical cadence with American ideals.
Two Australian moments.
On 10 December 1992, Prime Minister Paul Keating spoke in Redfern Park, Sydney, six months after the High Court's Mabo decision.
The speech, largely written by Don Watson, said plainly that non-Indigenous Australians had taken the land, brought the diseases and taken the children from their mothers.
Its power came from 'we': rather than blaming a distant past, it asked listeners to imagine these things done to them.
On 9 October 2012, Prime Minister Julia Gillard answered Tony Abbott in a roughly 15-minute speech, largely from notes, refusing to be lectured about sexism and misogyny by him.
Opinion in Australia was divided, but the video spread globally, and the Macquarie Dictionary soon broadened its definition of misogyny.
Common techniques.
Look across these speeches and patterns appear.
Repetition: 'we shall fight', 'I have a dream'.
Groups of three, like Lincoln's government 'of the people, by the people, for the people'.
Contrast, setting what is against what could be.
Concrete images: a bounced cheque, beaches and streets, children taken from their mothers.
Speechwriters also write for the ear: short sentences, strong verbs and deliberate pauses.
Many of these devices were catalogued by ancient Greek and Roman teachers of rhetoric, which is why a speech from 1863 and one from 2012 can feel related.
Moment and message.
None of these speeches worked in a vacuum.
Lincoln spoke amid a war whose purpose people questioned.
Churchill spoke when invasion seemed possible.
King spoke at the height of the civil rights movement.
Keating spoke just after Mabo overturned the legal fiction of terra nullius.
Gillard spoke after months of heated debate about her treatment as the first female prime minister.
The Greeks called this kairos: the right words at the right moment.
The same lessons work at a wedding, a team meeting or a funeral.
Be brief.
Build around one memorable line or image.
Acknowledge hard truths.
Speak to what the room feels.
Practise aloud.
The key idea: Lincoln's 270-word Gettysburg Address and Churchill's blunt 1940 speeches show that short, honest words can carry great weight.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does good persuasion usually combine ethos, pathos and logos?
Answer. Each mode covers weaknesses in the others.
Question two. Why do facts inside a story tend to stick better than a list of facts?
Answer. Its want, obstacle and change gives facts a shape.
Question three. Repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of successive phrases is an example of what?
Answer. Anaphora.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
